chosen.title: ADHD Isn't a Lack of Attention
chosen.angle: The name says 'deficit', but many researchers describe ADHD as trouble regulating attention: people with ADHD can lock onto things that interest them and still struggle to steer attention where they need it. Reframes the 'lazy / can't focus' myth without overclaiming. Educational, not medical advice.
chosen.hook: ADHD isn't a lack of attention. It's trouble steering it.
chosen.audience: curious adults, no jargon; includes people with ADHD and people who live or work with them

claims.claim: ADHD is a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that makes it hard to function in at least two areas of life (e.g. home, school, work).
Some researchers argue ADHD is better described as a disorder of attention regulation than of attention deficit (Hupfeld et al., 2019; Kooij et al., 2019).

People with ADHD report hyperfocus (deep absorption in enjoyable or rewarding activities) more often than people without ADHD (Hupfeld et al., 2019). Based on self-report; hyperfocus is not an official diagnostic criterion.
ADHD is highly heritable: mean heritability of 74% across 37 twin studies (Faraone & Larsson, 2019, Molecular Psychiatry 24:562-575).
About 6.0% of US adults (15.5 million) have ADHD; 55.9% of them received their first diagnosis in adulthood (CDC NCHS, 2023 survey).
There is no single test; diagnosis is a clinical assessment by a qualified professional.

chosen.notes: Source index: 0 NIMH (definition, assessment), 1 Hupfeld et al. 2019 line of work (regulation framing, hyperfocus), 2 Faraone & Larsson 2019 (heritability), 3 CDC/NCHS (prevalence, adult diagnosis). Say 'some researchers' and 'people report'; never 'ADHD is a superpower' and never give treatment advice. Add 'educational, not medical advice' in caption. Avoid 'signs you have ADHD' lists (encourages self-diagnosis). Off-niche (psychology/health) at the user's request.
